questions.why: Reported questions use statement order, so there is no inversion. 'Was it' keeps the question form.

questions.q: 'I have been waiting for an hour,' he said. Reported: He said that he ____ for an hour.
questions.why: Present perfect continuous backshifts to past perfect continuous. 'Has been waiting' does not shift, and 'was waited' is a passive form that makes no sense here.

questions.q: 'Don't forget to bring your passport,' my uncle said. Reported: My uncle reminded me ____ my passport.
questions.why: Remind + object takes a to-infinitive. A gerund or bare verb is not grammatical here.

questions.q: The minister announced, 'We will invest in rural schools next year.' Reported: The minister announced that the government ____ in rural schools the following year.
questions.why: Will backshifts to would, and 'next year' changes to 'the following year'. 'Had invested' would refer to the past.

questions.q: The journalist asked the mayor, 'Have you considered the environmental impact?' Reported: The journalist asked the mayor ____ the environmental impact.
questions.why: A yes/no question is reported with whether or if, statement order, and a backshift to past perfect. 'Had he considered' keeps the question inversion.

questions.q: The report states, 'Air pollution is a major cause of respiratory disease.' Reported: The report claims that air pollution ____ a major cause of respiratory disease.
questions.why: When the reporting verb is in the present tense, no backshift is needed. 'Was' would wrongly treat the report as already past.

questions.q: The professor said last year, 'Online learning has transformed education.' Reported: The professor said last year that online learning ____ education.
questions.why: Present perfect backshifts to past perfect after a past reporting verb. 'Was transformed' is passive and changes the meaning.

questions.q: 'You should have registered earlier,' the officer told the applicant. Reported: The officer told the applicant that he ____ earlier.
questions.why: Should have + past participle does not change in reported speech. 'Should register' loses the past reference and 'should had' is ungrammatical.

questions.q: Dr Hasan said, 'The students who participated were given a questionnaire.' Reported: Dr Hasan said that the students who participated ____ a questionnaire.
questions.why: Past simple passive backshifts to past perfect passive. 'Had given' is active and changes who performs the action.

questions.q: 'Please don't use mobile phones during the lecture,' the lecturer said. Reported: The lecturer asked the students ____ mobile phones during the lecture.
questions.why: Negative requests use 'not to + verb' after ask. The other options are ungrammatical.

questions.q: The spokesperson said last month, 'The factory has closed.' Reported: The spokesperson said last month that the factory ____.
questions.why: Present perfect backshifts to past perfect. 'Would close' turns a completed event into a future one.

questions.q: Critics argued at the time, 'The policy will widen inequality.' Reported: Critics argued at the time that the policy ____ inequality.
questions.why: Will backshifts to would after the past reporting verb 'argued'. 'Widened' and 'had widened' misplace the time of the prediction.

questions.q: Several parents ____ that the new curriculum was too demanding for younger pupils.
questions.why: Complain can be followed by a that-clause. Apologise, refuse and offer do not take a that-clause with this meaning.

title: Subject-Verb Agreement
summary: Covers making the verb agree with its real subject, including long noun phrases, either/or and neither/nor, collective and uncountable nouns, and expressions such as 'the number of'. Agreement errors are frequent in IELTS Writing and quickly lower the Grammatical Range and Accuracy band.

rules.rule: The verb agrees with the head noun of the subject, not the nearest noun.
rules.example: The cost of textbooks has risen sharply.

rules.rule: Phrases such as along with, as well as and together with do not change the subject.
rules.example: The teacher, along with the students, is attending the seminar.

rules.rule: Each, every, either, neither, everyone and nobody take a singular verb; 'a number of' is plural but 'the number of' is singular.
rules.example: Each of the candidates has a number, and the number of candidates is rising.

rules.rule: With either...or, neither...nor and not only...but also, the verb agrees with the nearer subject.
rules.example: Neither the manager nor the employees were informed.

rules.rule: Uncountable nouns and -ics subjects (information, equipment, news, economics) are singular, while police, people and scissors are plural.
rules.example: The information is useful, but the police are still investigating.

mistakes.wrong: The number of students have increased.
mistakes.right: The number of students has increased.
mistakes.why: 'The number of' is singular, so it takes 'has'.

mistakes.wrong: Each of the students have a laptop.
mistakes.right: Each of the students has a laptop.
mistakes.why: Each is singular even though 'students' is plural.

mistakes.wrong: The information are very useful.
mistakes.right: The information is very useful.
mistakes.why: Information is uncountable and takes a singular verb.

tip: In Writing Task 1, check the verb after phrases like 'the proportion of' and 'the number of', and in Task 2, re-check long subjects before the verb. In Speaking, slow down slightly in sentences with 'each of', 'a number of' and 'there is/are'.

questions.q: The students in my class ____ very hardworking.
questions.why: The subject 'students' is plural, so it needs 'are'. 'Is' agrees with the nearer singular noun 'class', which is a mistake.

questions.q: Each of the candidates ____ a separate booth for the speaking test.
questions.why: Each is singular, so it takes 'has'. 'Candidates' is plural but it is not the subject.

questions.q: My brother and my sister ____ both studying abroad.
questions.why: Two subjects joined by 'and' take a plural verb. 'Is' and 'has' are singular.

questions.q: The news from the ministry ____ encouraging.
questions.why: News is uncountable and singular despite the final 's'. 'Are' is a common mistake.

questions.q: Mathematics ____ my favourite subject at school.
questions.why: Subjects ending in -ics, such as mathematics, take a singular verb. 'Are' treats the word as plural.

questions.q: There ____ many tea gardens in Sylhet.
questions.why: After 'There', the verb agrees with the noun that follows. 'Tea gardens' is plural, so 'is' and 'was' are wrong.

questions.q: Everyone in the room ____ listening carefully.
questions.why: Everyone is singular and takes 'is'. 'Are' is wrongly influenced by the idea of many people.

questions.q: A number of students ____ absent today.
questions.why: 'A number of' means 'several' and takes a plural verb. 'The number of' would take a singular one.

questions.q: The price of vegetables ____ risen sharply this month.
questions.why: The subject is 'price', which is singular, not 'vegetables'. 'Have' agrees with the wrong noun.

questions.q: My father, along with his colleagues, ____ going to Chattogram.
questions.why: 'Along with' does not change the subject, which is the singular 'father'. 'Are' wrongly treats colleagues as part of the subject.

questions.q: Neither the manager nor the employees ____ aware of the change.
questions.why: With neither...nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'employees', which is plural. 'Was' agrees with the farther subject.

questions.q: The number of international students ____ increased since 2015.
questions.why: 'The number of' is singular and takes 'has'. 'Have' follows the plural noun 'students'.

questions.q: Either my cousins or my sister ____ coming to the airport.
questions.why: With either...or, the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'sister', which is singular. 'Are' agrees with the farther noun.

questions.q: Two-thirds of the farmers in this village ____ rice.
questions.why: Fractions take the number of the noun after 'of'. 'Farmers' is plural, so the verb is plural.

questions.q: Fifty thousand taka ____ a lot of money for a student.
questions.why: A sum of money is treated as a single amount and takes a singular verb. 'Are' treats each taka separately.

questions.q: The police ____ investigating the theft at the university.
questions.why: 'Police' is always plural, so it takes 'are'. 'Is' and 'has been' are singular.

questions.q: Economics, as well as statistics, ____ taught in the first year.
questions.why: 'As well as' does not change the subject, which is the singular noun 'economics'. 'Are' is influenced by the second subject.

questions.q: The scissors on the desk ____ mine.
questions.why: 'Scissors' is a plural noun that has no singular form, so it takes 'are'. 'Is' is only used with 'a pair of scissors'.

questions.q: Not only the lecturer but also the students ____ pleased with the result.
questions.why: With not only...but also, the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'students'. 'Was' agrees with the singular 'lecturer'.

questions.q: Everything that the speakers said ____ interesting.
questions.why: Everything is singular and the context is past, so 'was' is correct. 'Were' and 'are' are plural forms.

questions.q: The rapid growth of low-cost airlines, together with rising incomes, ____ led to a surge in international tourism.
questions.why: 'Together with' does not change the subject. The head noun 'growth' is singular, so 'has' is correct.

questions.q: A large proportion of the graduates in this field ____ unemployed for more than a year.
questions.why: With proportions, the verb agrees with the noun after 'of'. 'Graduates' is plural, so 'remain' is correct.

questions.q: The findings of the survey, which was conducted among 2,000 teenagers, ____ that social media use affects concentration.
questions.why: The subject is 'findings', which is plural. The singular 'survey' inside the relative clause misleads some learners into choosing 'suggests'.

questions.q: Neither the government's proposals nor the opposition's amendments ____ likely to resolve the shortage of teachers.
questions.why: With neither...nor, the verb agrees with the nearer noun, 'amendments', which is plural. 'Seems' follows the singular pattern.

questions.q: The rise in the number of electric vehicles ____ expected to reduce urban air pollution.
questions.why: The head noun is 'rise', which is singular. 'Vehicles' and 'number' are inside prepositional phrases and do not control the verb.

questions.q: Each of the proposed solutions to the energy crisis ____ its own drawbacks.
questions.why: Each is singular and takes 'has'. 'Have' is attracted by the plural 'solutions'.

questions.q: The equipment used in the laboratory ____ regularly updated.
questions.why: Equipment is uncountable, so it takes a singular verb. 'Are' and 'were' wrongly treat it as plural.

questions.q: Science and technology ____ played a vital role in improving healthcare.
questions.why: Two subjects joined by 'and' take a plural verb. 'Has' would only be used if both formed one single idea.

questions.q: One of the main reasons why students drop out of university ____ financial pressure.
questions.why: The subject is 'One', which is singular. 'Reasons' is part of a phrase after 'of' and does not control the verb.

questions.q: The team of researchers, led by two professors from Dhaka University, ____ published its findings in an international journal.
questions.why: The singular noun 'team' is the subject, and the pronoun 'its' confirms that it is treated as a unit. 'Have' is mismatched with 'its'.

title: Linking words and cohesion
summary: Covers conjunctions and linking phrases used to show addition, contrast, cause, result, purpose and condition. In IELTS Writing and Speaking, accurate linking is central to Coherence and Cohesion and to sentence control in Grammar.

rules.rule: Use 'although', 'even though' and 'while' with a full clause; use 'despite' and 'in spite of' with a noun or -ing form.
rules.example: Although the fees were high, many families paid them. Despite the high fees, many families paid them.

rules.rule: Sentence adverbs such as 'however', 'therefore' and 'moreover' start a new sentence (or follow a semicolon) and are followed by a comma.
rules.example: The scheme is popular; however, it is expensive.

rules.rule: Match the linker to the logic: addition (moreover), contrast (whereas), cause (because), result (consequently), purpose (so that), condition (unless).
rules.example: Unless governments act now, air quality will worsen.

rules.rule: Do not join two main clauses with only a comma; add a conjunction (and, but, so) or use a semicolon or full stop.
rules.example: The roads flooded, so schools closed for a week.

rules.rule: Vary your linkers and do not overuse them; clear reference words (this, such, these) also create cohesion.
rules.example: Many students lack internet access. This problem is serious in rural areas.

mistakes.wrong: Despite of the rain, the match continued.
mistakes.right: Despite the rain, the match continued.
mistakes.why: 'Despite' is never followed by 'of'; use 'in spite of' if you want 'of'.

mistakes.wrong: Although the exam was hard, but I passed.
mistakes.right: Although the exam was hard, I passed.
mistakes.why: 'Although' and 'but' both show contrast; use only one.

mistakes.wrong: Many people use cars. However they cause pollution.
mistakes.right: Many people use cars. However, they cause pollution.
mistakes.why: A sentence-initial linker needs a comma after it.

tip: In Writing Task 2, plan one clear linker per paragraph connection (for example, concession in the counter-argument) instead of starting every sentence with 'Moreover' or 'However'. In Speaking, use simple linkers such as 'because', 'although' and 'on the other hand' accurately rather than rare ones.

questions.q: Dhaka is crowded; ____, many people still move there for jobs.
questions.why: The second clause contrasts with crowding, so a contrast linker is needed. 'Therefore' would wrongly show a result.

questions.q: She studied hard ____ she wanted a high band score.
questions.why: The second clause gives the reason for studying hard. 'Although' and 'but' show contrast, which does not fit.

questions.q: ____ it was raining, the students walked to the exam centre.
questions.why: The walking happened in spite of the rain, so a concession word is needed. 'Because' gives a reason that makes no sense here.

questions.q: The bus was late. ____, I missed the first part of the lecture.
questions.why: Missing the lecture is the consequence of the late bus. 'In contrast' would introduce an opposite idea, and 'Despite' cannot start a new sentence like this.

questions.q: He speaks Bangla ____ English fluently.
questions.why: Both languages are added together, so 'and' is correct. 'But' would suggest a contrast that is not there.

questions.q: You will not pass ____ you practise regularly.
questions.why: 'Unless' means 'if not'. With 'if' the sentence would say the opposite of what is intended.

questions.q: First, boil the water. ____, add the rice.
questions.why: 'Then' shows the next step in a sequence. 'However' signals a contrast, which is not logical in instructions.

questions.q: ____ the heavy traffic, we arrived on time.
questions.why: 'Despite' is followed by a noun phrase ('the heavy traffic'). 'Although' needs a full clause, so it is wrong here.

questions.q: Online learning is flexible. ____, students can study at midnight if they wish.
questions.why: The second sentence gives a specific example of flexibility. The other options express contrast.

questions.q: He was tired, ____ he continued working.
questions.why: Continuing despite tiredness is a contrast, so 'but' fits. 'So' would suggest tiredness caused him to work, which is illogical.

questions.q: Sales fell sharply; ____, the firm closed two branches.
questions.why: Closing branches is the result of falling sales. 'Nevertheless' would signal an unexpected contrast.

questions.q: Urban areas have good hospitals, ____ rural areas often lack them.
questions.why: 'Whereas' compares two contrasting situations in one sentence. 'Because' wrongly makes one the cause of the other.

questions.q: She took notes ____ she would remember the lecture.
questions.why: 'So that' expresses purpose. 'As long as' states a condition, and 'such that' is not used this way.

questions.q: ____ the new policy was popular, it was soon cancelled.
questions.why: Cancellation is surprising given the popularity, so a concession clause is needed. 'Because' would imply popularity caused the cancellation.

questions.q: Students may use phones in class ____ they switch them to silent.
questions.why: 'Provided that' introduces a condition. 'Although' would make the permission contrast with the silent setting, which is illogical.

questions.q: The course is cheap. ____, it is flexible.
questions.why: The second sentence adds another advantage. 'Nevertheless' would wrongly treat flexibility as a contrast.

questions.q: Revise daily; ____, you may forget key vocabulary.
questions.why: 'Otherwise' means 'if you do not', showing a negative consequence. 'Therefore' would give a result of revising, which is the opposite.

questions.q: Rice prices rose. ____, farmers' incomes did not improve.
questions.why: Incomes not improving is unexpected after higher prices, so a concession link is needed. 'Therefore' would show cause and result.

questions.q: ____ the cost, many families chose private tutoring.
questions.why: The fixed phrase is 'in spite of' or 'despite' with no 'of'. 'Although' cannot be followed by a noun phrase.

questions.q: He did not blame the teacher; ____, he blamed himself.
questions.why: 'Instead' replaces the first idea with the second. 'Moreover' only adds, and does not show replacement.

questions.q: Some argue that remote work boosts productivity; ____, others claim it isolates employees.
questions.why: The two views are opposed, so 'conversely' is right. 'Likewise' would signal agreement.

questions.q: Carbon taxes may cut emissions. ____, they risk burdening low-income households.
questions.why: The second sentence adds a drawback, so a concession phrase fits. 'Hence' and 'Thus' show result.

questions.q: Literacy rates have risen sharply, ____ access to quality schooling remains uneven.
questions.why: 'Yet' joins two contrasting facts. 'For' means 'because' and would give a false reason.

questions.q: The policy was introduced to reduce congestion; ____, travel times have barely changed.
questions.why: The outcome contradicts the aim, so 'nevertheless' is correct. 'Accordingly' would suggest the result matched the plan.

questions.q: Antibiotics are often overprescribed. ____, drug-resistant bacteria are spreading.
questions.why: Spread of resistance is the effect of overprescription. 'Admittedly' and 'conversely' signal concession and contrast.

questions.q: ____ renewable energy is costly to install, it is cheaper over time.
questions.why: 'While' here means 'although', joining a drawback with a benefit. 'Because' would make the high cost the reason for lower long-term cost.

questions.q: Universities should invest in mental health services, ____ student dropout rates are rising.
questions.why: Rising dropout is an additional reason supporting the claim. 'Whereas' would wrongly contrast the two ideas.

questions.q: Automation will not eliminate jobs entirely; ____, it will transform the skills demanded.
questions.why: 'Rather' corrects the first idea with a better statement. 'Hence' would claim the transformation results from jobs not being eliminated.

questions.q: Not only did the trial reduce costs, ____ it improved patient satisfaction.
questions.why: 'Not only ... but also' is the correct paired structure. 'As well' cannot complete it, and 'whereas' is a contrast word.

questions.q: ____ the evidence is limited, the findings suggest a link between sleep and memory.
questions.why: The findings are offered despite weak evidence, so a concession word fits. 'Unless' would create an illogical condition.

title: Word formation
summary: Covers how to build nouns, verbs, adjectives and adverbs using prefixes and suffixes, and how to choose the right word class for a sentence. IELTS rewards a wide, accurate range of vocabulary, and wrong forms are a common cause of lost marks in Writing and Speaking.

rules.rule: Identify the word class the gap needs: nouns follow articles and adjectives, adjectives follow 'be' and linking verbs, adverbs modify verbs and adjectives.
rules.example: The government made a significant decision, and it acted quickly.

rules.rule: Common noun suffixes: -tion, -ment, -ness, -ity, -ence/-ance, -er/-or (person). Check if a person, a thing or an idea is meant.
rules.example: Her determination and the tutor's guidance led to improvement.

rules.rule: Common adjective suffixes: -ful, -less, -ous, -able/-ible, -al, -ive, -ic. Use -ed for a feeling and -ing for what causes it.
rules.example: The students were bored because the lesson was boring.

rules.rule: Negative prefixes change meaning: un-, in-, im-, il-, ir-, dis-, mis-. Choose the one that matches the base word.
rules.example: It is impossible to finish; the plan is inadequate and unrealistic.

rules.rule: Do not just add a suffix to every word; some words have irregular forms and verbs come from adjectives with -en or -ise.
rules.example: Education can widen opportunities and strengthen communities.

mistakes.wrong: She is very interest in science.
mistakes.right: She is very interested in science.
mistakes.why: A feeling needs the -ed adjective, not the base verb.

mistakes.wrong: Pollute is a major problem in cities.
mistakes.right: Pollution is a major problem in cities.
mistakes.why: The subject must be a noun, so use 'pollution'.

mistakes.wrong: He works very hardly.
mistakes.right: He works very hard.
mistakes.why: 'Hard' is both adjective and adverb; 'hardly' means 'almost not'.

tip: Before writing a key word in Task 2, ask yourself which word class the gap needs, then build it from one root (for example, employ, employment, unemployed). Using accurate word forms shows Lexical Resource and avoids Grammar errors.

questions.q: Her ____ in English improved after the course.
questions.why: After 'her' we need a noun. 'Fluency' is the noun form of 'fluent'.

questions.q: He answered the question ____.
questions.why: An adverb is needed to modify the verb 'answered'. 'Correct' is an adjective.

questions.q: Education is ____ for every child.
questions.why: After 'is' we need an adjective. 'Essentially' is an adverb and 'essentials' is a plural noun.

questions.q: Smoking is ____ to health.
questions.why: After 'is' we need an adjective. 'Danger' is a noun and would need 'a danger to health'.

questions.q: The ____ who planned the event were thanked.
questions.why: 'Who' refers to people, so a person noun is needed. 'Organisation' is a thing or body, not the people planning.

questions.q: Unlike his brother, he is very ____ and never takes risks.
questions.why: After 'is very' we need an adjective. 'Carefully' is an adverb and cannot follow 'is' here.

questions.q: She was ____ with her exam results.
questions.why: A person's feeling uses the -ed adjective. 'Disappointing' describes the thing that causes the feeling.

questions.q: The ____ between the two cities is 200 km.
questions.why: After 'The' we need a singular noun matching 'is'. 'Distant' is an adjective and 'distances' does not agree with 'is'.

questions.q: It is ____ to cross the road without looking.
questions.why: The meaning is negative, so the prefix 'un-' is needed. 'Wise' would mean the opposite.

questions.q: The teacher gave clear ____ before the test.
questions.why: After the adjective 'clear' we need a noun. 'Instructions' is the noun for the directions given.

questions.q: Mobile banking has ____ access to financial services.
questions.why: 'Has' needs a past participle, so the verb 'widened' is required. 'Wide' and 'widely' are adjective and adverb.

questions.q: His ____ to the company was rewarded with a promotion.
questions.why: After 'His' and before 'was' we need a singular noun. 'Loyalties' is plural and does not agree with 'was'.

questions.q: The medicine is only ____ if taken regularly.
questions.why: After 'is only' we need an adjective. 'Effectiveness' is a noun and cannot describe the medicine.

questions.q: A detailed ____ of the data took three weeks.
questions.why: After 'detailed' and before 'of' we need a noun for the process. 'Analyst' is a person, which does not fit.

questions.q: Rapid ____ has increased pressure on housing.
questions.why: The subject after the adjective 'Rapid' must be a noun. 'Urbanisation' names the process.

questions.q: Many graduates remain ____ despite their qualifications.
questions.why: 'Remain' is followed by an adjective here. 'Unemployment' is a noun and would mean the graduates are a condition.

questions.q: She spoke so ____ that nobody could hear her.
questions.why: An adverb is needed to modify the verb 'spoke'. 'Quiet' is an adjective.

questions.q: The new law aims to ____ women in the workplace.
questions.why: After 'to' we need a base verb. 'Empowerment' is a noun and 'powerful' is an adjective.

questions.q: Their ____ on foreign aid is a concern.
questions.why: After 'Their' we need a noun, followed by 'on'. 'Dependent' is an adjective and cannot be the subject.

questions.q: The documentary was ____ and changed my views.
questions.why: A thing that causes the effect takes the -ing adjective. 'Enlightened' would describe a person.

questions.q: Researchers have emphasised the ____ of early intervention.
questions.why: After 'the' we need a noun. 'Importance' is the noun form; 'imports' has a different meaning.

questions.q: The ____ of renewable energy has reduced reliance on fossil fuels.
questions.why: After 'The' and before 'of' we need a noun. 'Adopted' is a verb or adjective form and cannot follow this pattern.

questions.q: Critics regard the scheme as ____ because it ignores rural needs.
questions.why: The reason given is negative, so the negative adjective is needed. 'Adequate' would contradict the reason.

questions.q: Increased ____ among teenagers is partly attributed to social media.
questions.why: After 'Increased' we need an uncountable noun matching 'is'. 'Anxieties' is plural and does not agree with 'is'.

questions.q: The findings are ____ with earlier research.
questions.why: After 'are' we need an adjective followed by 'with'. 'Consistently' is an adverb and would not fit this pattern.

questions.q: Governments must ensure that vaccines are ____ to all citizens.
questions.why: After 'are' we need an adjective. 'Accessibility' is a noun and cannot describe the vaccines.

questions.q: Many employees feel ____ when tasks are repetitive.
questions.why: After 'feel' we need an adjective describing the person's state, with a negative meaning. 'Motivating' describes the task, not the employee.

questions.q: The ____ of antibiotics has led to resistant strains.
questions.why: After 'The' and before 'of' a noun is needed. 'Overusing' and 'overused' are verb forms that do not fit.

questions.q: Teachers need to be ____ to the diverse needs of learners.
questions.why: The collocation is 'sensitive to'. 'Sensible' means practical and is not followed by 'to' in this meaning.

questions.q: The ____ of this approach is questionable, as no trials have confirmed it.
questions.why: After 'The' and before 'of' we need a noun. 'Valid' and 'invalid' are adjectives.

title: Sentence structure and punctuation: fragments, run-ons, complex sentences
summary: Covers how to build complete sentences, avoid fragments, run-ons and comma splices, and combine clauses using relative pronouns and subordinators. IELTS Grammatical Range and Accuracy rewards a mix of simple and complex sentences that are error-free.

rules.rule: A complete sentence needs a subject and a finite verb and must express a complete idea; a clause starting with 'because', 'although' or 'which' alone is a fragment.
rules.example: Because the bridge collapsed, traffic stopped for hours.

rules.rule: Do not join two main clauses with a comma alone; use a conjunction, a semicolon or a full stop.
rules.example: The river flooded; the villagers moved to higher ground.

rules.rule: Use relative pronouns correctly: who for people, which for things, that for defining clauses, whose for possession.
rules.example: The teacher whose class I joined has won an award.

rules.rule: Non-defining relative clauses are set off by commas; defining clauses are not.
rules.example: Bangladesh, which has a large population, faces housing pressure.

rules.rule: Keep lists and paired structures parallel, and put a modifier next to the word it describes.
rules.example: She plans to study, work and travel.

mistakes.wrong: Because he was late.
mistakes.right: Because he was late, he missed the bus.
mistakes.why: A 'because' clause alone is a fragment and needs a main clause.

mistakes.wrong: Online learning is popular, it is cheap.
mistakes.right: Online learning is popular, and it is cheap.
mistakes.why: Two main clauses joined only by a comma form a comma splice.

mistakes.wrong: Walking home, the rain started.
mistakes.right: Walking home, I felt the rain start.
mistakes.why: The opening phrase must describe the subject that follows; rain cannot walk.

tip: In Writing Task 2, aim for a mix: one or two simple sentences for clarity and several complex sentences with relative or concession clauses. Before submitting, check each long sentence for a main clause and for any comma splice. In Speaking, extend answers with 'because', 'which' and 'although' while keeping sentences complete.

questions.q: Which of these is a complete sentence?
options: Walking to the library every day.
questions.why: Only this option has a subject and a finite verb and expresses a complete idea. The others are fragments that depend on missing clauses.

questions.q: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: I was tired I went to bed early.
I was tired, so I went to bed early.
I was tired, I went to bed early.
I was tired so, I went to bed early.
questions.why: Two main clauses need a conjunction after a comma. Without it the sentence is a run-on or comma splice.

questions.q: She wanted to study abroad, ____ her family could not afford it.
questions.why: The second clause is a contrast with her wish. 'So' would mean the cost was the result of wanting to study abroad.

questions.q: ____ the road was closed, we reached the village by boat.
questions.why: We reached the village in spite of the closed road. 'Despite' cannot be followed by a full clause.

questions.q: My brother ____ lives in Sylhet works as a doctor.
questions.why: 'Who' refers to a person and acts as the subject of 'lives'. 'Whom' is for objects and 'which' is for things.

questions.q: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: I bought rice lentils and fish.
I bought rice, lentils and fish.
I bought, rice, lentils and fish.
I bought rice; lentils; and fish.
questions.why: Items in a list are separated by commas, with 'and' before the last one. The other versions misplace or omit punctuation.

questions.q: She is tired ____ she worked all night.
questions.why: The second clause explains the reason for tiredness. 'So' would reverse cause and effect.

questions.q: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: The test was long, however most students finished.
The test was long however; most students finished.
The test was long however, most students finished.
The test was long; however, most students finished.
questions.why: A semicolon before 'however' and a comma after it correctly joins two main clauses. The others create comma splices or misplace punctuation.

questions.q: Which group of words is a fragment?
questions.why: It has a subject and verb but begins with 'Because', so it cannot stand alone. The other options are complete sentences.

questions.q: He is the student ____ essay won the prize.
questions.why: 'Whose' shows possession: the student's essay. 'Who' cannot be followed directly by 'essay' here.

questions.q: The book ____ I borrowed from the library was very useful.
questions.why: A defining clause about a thing uses 'that'. 'Who' is for people, and 'whose' shows possession.

questions.q: Which sentence is a run-on?
options: The road flooded, so we stayed home.
We stayed home because the road flooded.
The road flooded; we stayed home.
The road flooded we stayed home.
questions.why: Two main clauses are joined with no punctuation or conjunction. The other three are correctly joined.

questions.q: Which sentence uses a semicolon correctly?
options: Rain fell all night; the roads flooded.
I like tea; and she likes coffee.
The reason is; that he was ill.
questions.why: A semicolon links two complete main clauses. The other options use it after a dependent clause or in the middle of a clause.

questions.q: Not only ____ the course teach grammar, but it also builds vocabulary.
questions.why: After 'Not only' at the start we use inversion with the auxiliary. 'Course' is singular and the verb is present, so 'does'.

questions.q: Neither the teacher nor the students ____ aware of the change.
questions.why: With 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'students', which is plural.

questions.q: She enjoys reading, writing and ____.
questions.why: Items in a list must have the same grammatical form, here -ing forms.

questions.q: The man ____ I met yesterday is my new tutor.
questions.why: 'Whom' is the object of 'met' and refers to a person. 'Whose' would show possession.

questions.q: Which sentence is complex?
options: The exam was hard, and I was nervous.
Because it was late, we went home.
We studied, but we failed; we tried again.
questions.why: A complex sentence has a main clause and a dependent clause, here introduced by 'Because'. The other options are simple or compound.

questions.q: If I ____ more time, I would revise again.
questions.why: The second conditional uses past simple in the 'if' clause and 'would' in the result clause.

questions.q: Which uses the colon correctly?
options: She packed: a passport, a ticket and a bag.
She packed three: things a passport, a ticket and a bag.
She packed three things, : a passport, a ticket and a bag.
She packed three things: a passport, a ticket and a bag.
questions.why: A colon follows a complete clause and introduces the list. The first alternative interrupts the verb and its object.

questions.q: The policy, ____ was introduced in 2019, has reduced plastic waste.
questions.why: A non-defining clause set off by commas uses 'which'. 'That' is not used after a comma in this way.

questions.q: Walking through the village, ____.
options: an old mosque caught my eye
questions.why: The opening phrase must refer to the subject that is walking. Only 'I' did the walking; the others leave a dangling modifier.

questions.q: Rarely ____ such rapid technological change been observed.
questions.why: After a negative adverb at the start, we invert the auxiliary. The subject 'change' is singular, so 'has'.

questions.q: Students ____ attendance is low are unlikely to improve.
questions.why: 'Whose' shows possession (their attendance). 'Who' cannot be followed by a noun phrase like this.

questions.q: The programme aims to reduce costs, improve quality and ____ access.
questions.why: The list follows 'to', so the verbs must be parallel base forms: reduce, improve, widen.

questions.q: Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
options: The study, which involved 2,000 adults found that sleep improves memory.
The study which involved 2,000 adults, found that sleep improves memory.
The study, which involved 2,000 adults, found that sleep improves memory.
The study, which involved 2,000 adults found, that sleep improves memory.
questions.why: A non-defining clause needs commas on both sides. The other versions omit or misplace one.

questions.q: Had the government acted earlier, the damage ____ avoided.
questions.why: This is an inverted third conditional about a past situation, so the result uses 'could have been'.

questions.q: The number of students who study abroad ____ increasing.
questions.why: The subject is 'the number' (singular), not 'students'. 'Is' agrees with it.

questions.q: Which sentence avoids a comma splice?
options: Online courses are flexible, they are also cheaper.
Online courses are flexible; they are also cheaper.
Online courses are flexible they are also cheaper.
Online courses are flexible, however they are cheaper.
questions.why: A semicolon correctly joins two independent clauses. The others use only a comma or no punctuation.

questions.q: It is essential that every student ____ a copy of the form.
questions.why: After 'essential that', the subjunctive uses the base form of the verb regardless of subject.
